RAG architecture: How would you design a: Chunk along semantic boundaries (sections/paragraphs) rather than fixed character counts, with modest overlap so answers spanning a boundary aren't lost; choose an embedding model matched to the domain and language needs, benchmarked on your actual data rather than assumed from a leaderboard; pick a vector database based on scale/latency/operational needs (pgvector for simplicity if already on Postgres, a dedicated service like Pinecone/Weaviate for larger scale or advanced filtering). Add a re-ranking step (a cross-encoder re-scoring the top-k retrieved candidates) since embedding similarity alone often surfaces near-misses that a re-ranker filters out. Measure retrieval quality directly with a labeled evaluation set (question -> expected source chunk) tracking recall@k, not just eyeballing a few example answers - this is the only way to know if a chunking/model change actually helped.
LLM serving on Kubernetes: How would you: Provision a GPU node pool sized to the model (accelerator type/count matched to model size and target throughput), with taints/tolerations so only LLM-serving Pods land there. Use vLLM or TGI's built-in continuous batching (dynamically grouping concurrent requests to maximize GPU utilization, rather than one request per forward pass) for meaningfully better throughput. Scale via HPA on a custom metric reflecting actual load (queue depth or in-flight request count, not CPU, since GPU-bound inference doesn't correlate with CPU usage), and handle bursty load with an explicit request queue in front of the serving layer with backpressure (returning a fast, clear error or a 429 rather than accepting unbounded requests that degrade latency for everyone) since GPU capacity can't scale as instantly as CPU-based autoscaling.
Prompt injection and guardrails: How wou: Layer defenses rather than relying on any single one: input classification to flag/block suspicious patterns before they reach the model, strict system-prompt design that clearly separates trusted instructions from untrusted user/retrieved content (and instructs the model to treat retrieved content as data, not instructions), output validation/guardrails (a second model pass or a framework like Llama Guard checking responses before they reach the user or trigger a tool call), and - critically for tool-calling agents - never letting the model's output directly trigger a high-risk action without validation; scope tool permissions tightly (least privilege) so even a successful injection can't do meaningful damage, and log every tool call for audit and anomaly detection.
Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompt engineering: Start with prompt engineering - it's the cheapest and fastest to iterate, and solves a surprising amount if the model already has the needed knowledge/capability and just needs better instructions/examples. Move to RAG when the problem is missing or dynamic knowledge (facts the model wasn't trained on, or that change frequently) - it's more expensive to build than prompting but far cheaper to keep updated than fine-tuning. Reserve fine-tuning for when you need to change the model's consistent behavior/format/style across every call, or teach a narrow skill prompting can't reliably achieve - it's the most expensive and slowest-to-iterate option, and doesn't solve a knowledge gap the way RAG does, so the three aren't strictly interchangeable, they solve different problems.
Cost and latency optimization: An LLM fe: Start with caching (prompt/context caching for shared prefixes, response caching for repeated queries) since it's often the single highest-impact, lowest-effort lever. Add model routing - use a small, fast, cheap model for simple steps (classification, extraction) and reserve the large model only for steps that genuinely need its reasoning capability, rather than one model for everything. Quantization (running a smaller-precision version of a self-hosted model) reduces cost/latency with a quality tradeoff worth validating against your eval suite. Batching improves throughput/cost efficiency for self-hosted serving. Streaming doesn't reduce actual cost/total latency but dramatically improves perceived latency by showing tokens as they're generated - worth doing regardless for UX even if it's not a true cost fix.
LLM evaluation in CI: How would you eval: Maintain a versioned golden dataset of representative inputs with expected properties or a rubric, and run it automatically in CI on every prompt/model change - scoring with automated metrics where objective (schema validity, exact match for structured tasks) plus an LLM-as-judge pass for subjective quality (helpfulness, faithfulness) against the rubric. Treat any regression against the current production version's score as a blocking CI failure, exactly like a test suite, and keep growing the golden set with real production failures you've observed so evaluation reflects actual failure modes rather than only anticipated ones.
Vector database operations: How would yo: Choose an index type matched to the scale/recall-vs-speed tradeoff needed (HNSW for good recall at reasonable speed for most use cases, IVF for larger scale with a tunable accuracy tradeoff), and re-index or use incremental update support as data changes rather than requiring a full rebuild for every update if avoidable. Design freshness explicitly - decide whether near-real-time updates are needed (streaming ingestion into the vector store) or a scheduled batch re-embedding/upsert is acceptable, since this significantly affects architecture complexity. Back up the underlying data/embeddings (not just rely on the vector index alone, which may be rebuildable from source data anyway), and at scale, watch cost drivers specifically - embedding dimension size, total vector count, and query volume - since vector database costs can grow faster than teams expect as the corpus grows.
Agentic systems: For a multi-step, tool-: Observability: trace every step of every agent run (prompt, tool calls with arguments/results, reasoning, token cost, latency) so any bad outcome is fully explainable after the fact, not a mystery. Failure handling: validate every tool call's arguments before execution, catch and gracefully handle tool failures (feeding the error back to the agent to retry/adjust rather than crashing the whole run), and cap max iterations/tool calls per task as a hard circuit breaker. Guardrails: gate any destructive or high-risk action behind explicit human approval regardless of how confident the agent seems, scope tool credentials to least-privilege so even a runaway agent can't reach beyond what it should, and track cumulative token/cost spend per run with a hard abort threshold so a stuck loop fails fast and visibly rather than silently consuming unbounded budget.
